verses.zh: 看哪，必有一王凭公义行政；必有首领藉公平掌权。
verses.en: Look, a king will promote fairness;[NOTE:1] officials will promote justice.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “will reign according to fairness.”
Heb “will rule according to justice.”
verses.commentary:
32:1 "a king. . .princes" Isaiah 32:1-8 reflects the reign of a godly king and his/His government
(cf. Isa. 9:6-7; 11:1-5; 16:5; Jer. 23:5; 33:15; Micah 5:2-5a). There seems to be a purposeful ambiguity so that
Hezekiah (possibly the immediate fulfillment of Isa. 7:14-15) and the coming Messiah (the ultimate fulfillment,
cf. Isa. 7:14, cf. Matt. 1:23) are both reflected in this passage.

The leadership of Israel goes by several titles. For a good brief discussion, see Robert
Girdlestone, Synonyms of the Old Testament, p. 249-251.

verses.zh: 必有一人像避风所和避暴雨的隐密处，又像河流在干旱之地，像大磐石的影子在疲乏之地。
verses.en: Each of them[NOTE:1] will be like a shelter from the windand a refuge from a rainstorm;like streams of water in a dry regionand like the shade of a large cliff in a parched land.
notes: Heb “a man,” but אִישׁ (ʾish) probably refers here to “each” of the officials mentioned in the previous verse.
verses.commentary:
32:2 This verse describes in "desert" imagery the reign of this godly leader and his associates.

- a refuge (BDB 285, lit. "hiding place," this form is found only here) from the wind

- shelter (BDB 712) from the storm (parallel to #1)

- streams of water in a dry country

- the shade (BDB 853) of a huge rock in a parched land

Similar imagery is used of YHWH in Isa. 25:4. Now they describe all of God's people or at
least the leadership (i.e., "rulers will rule," VERB, BDB 979,
KB 1362, Qal IMPERFECT).

The VERB "each will be" (BDB 224, KB 243 Qal
PERFECT with waw) could refer to "the princes" of Isa. 32:1 or to the people of
the "new covenant" described in Jer. 31:31-34; Ezek. 36:22-36.

verses.zh: 那能看的人，眼不再昏迷；能听的人，耳必得听闻。
verses.en: Eyes[NOTE:1] will no longer be blind[NOTE:2] and ears[NOTE:3] will be attentive.
notes: Heb “Eyes that see.”

The Hebrew text as vocalized reads literally “will not gaze,” but this is contradictory to the context. The verb form should be revocalized as תְּשֹׁעֶינָה (teshoʿenah) from שָׁעַע (shʿaʿa, “be blinded”); see Isa 6:10; 29:9.
Heb “ears that hear.”
verses.commentary:
32:3-4 This reflects the spiritual condition of the restored covenant people as contrasted with
Isa. 6:9-10 (cf. Deut. 29:4).

- they will see

- they will hear

- they will discern truth

- they will speak truth ("the stammerers," BDB 748, occurs only here)

verses.zh: 冒失人的心必明白知识；结巴人的舌必说话通快。
verses.en: The mind that acts rashly will possess discernment,[NOTE:1] and the tongue that stutters will speak with ease and clarity.
notes: Heb “the heart of rashness will understand knowledge”; cf. NAB “The flighty will become wise and capable.”

verses.zh: 愚顽人不再称为高明；吝啬人不再称为大方。
verses.en: A fool will no longer be called honorable;a deceiver will no longer be called principled.
verses.commentary:
32:5-8 "fool. . .rogue" These two groups will still be present in society, but they will be seen for
what they are (Isa. 32:6-7). Isaiah 32:6-7 seems to describe the two wicked persons, while Isa. 32:8
describes the "true" noble person.

- the "fool" (BDB 614) described in Isa. 32:6

- speaks nonsense

- inclines the heart toward wickedness

(1) practices ungodliness (or "plots evil")

(2) speaks error against the Lord

- does not feed the hungry

- does not give drink to the thirsty

- the "rogue" (BDB 647, found only here, twice) described in Isa. 32:7

- has evil weapons

- devises wicked schemes

- destroys the afflicted with slander

- disregards the true testimony of the needy

- the noble man (BDB 622), Isa. 32:8

- devises noble (or "generous") plans in contrast to those mentioned in Isa. 32:6 and 7

- his plans stand, remain

verses.zh: 因为愚顽人必说愚顽话，心里想作罪孽，惯行亵渎的事，说错谬的话攻击耶和华，使饥饿的人无食可吃，使口渴的人无水可喝。
verses.en: For a fool speaks disgraceful things;[NOTE:1] his mind plans out sinful deeds.[NOTE:2] He commits godless deeds[NOTE:3] and says misleading things about the Lord;he gives the hungry nothing to satisfy their appetite[NOTE:4] and gives the thirsty nothing to drink.[NOTE:5]
notes: Or “foolishness,” in a moral-ethical sense. See 9:17.
Heb “and his heart commits sin”; KJV, ASV “his heart will work iniquity”; NASB “inclines toward wickedness.”
Heb “in order to do [or “so that he does”] what is godless [or “defiled”].”
Heb “so that he leaves empty the appetite [or “desire”] of the hungry.”
Heb “and the drink of the thirsty he causes to fail.”
verses.commentary:
32:6 One wonders if this is alluded to in Matt. 25:31-46.

▣ "inclines toward. . .to practice" The VERB (BDB 793, KB 889)
is used twice in this verse, once as a Qal IMPERFECT and again as a
Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT. This was a grammatical way to show
intensity. The "fool" tries to convey a false message about Israel's God and His will for an
obedient covenant people.

verses.zh: 吝啬人所用的法子是恶的；他图谋恶计，用谎言毁灭谦卑人；穷乏人讲公理的时候，他也是这样行。
verses.en: A deceiver’s methods are evil;[NOTE:1] he dreams up evil plans[NOTE:2] to ruin the poor with lies,even when the needy are in the right.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “as for a deceiver, his implements [or “weapons”] are evil.”
Or “he plans evil things”; NIV11 “they make up evil schemes.”
Heb “to ruin the poor with words of falsehood, even when the needy speak what is just.”

verses.zh: 高明人却谋高明事，在高明事上也必永存。
verses.en: An honorable man makes honorable plans;his honorable character gives him security.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “and he upon honorable things stands.”

verses.zh: 安逸的妇女啊，起来听我的声音！无虑的女子啊，侧耳听我的言语！
verses.en: You complacent[NOTE:1] women,get up and listen to me!You carefree[NOTE:2] daughters,pay attention to what I say!
notes: Or “self-assured”; NASB, NRSV “who are at ease.”
Or “self-confident”; NAB “overconfident.”
verses.commentary:
32:9-12 This strophe speaks of the rich, wealthy society women of Jerusalem (cf Isa. 3:16-4:1; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: WEALTH). The Jewish Study Bible, p. 847, notes that
this is a counterpoint to the condemnation of male leaders in Isa. 30:1-7; 31:1-3. Notice how they are addressed.

- rise up you women who are at ease, Isa. 32:9, BDB 877, KB 1086, Qal
IMPERATIVE. The same VERB was used in the previous verse
in the sense of "stand" or "remain," but here it means "stand up" when I the Lord
(or His prophet) address you.

- hear my voice, Isa. 32:9, BDB 1033, KB 1570, Qal IMPERATIVE

- give an ear to my word, Isa. 32:9, BDB 24, KB 27, Hiphil IMPERATIVE
(cf. Isa. 28:23). Notice how the second and third VERBS are parallel,
as are the descriptive phrases "women who are at ease," (cf. Isa. 32:11) and "you complacent
daughters," and again in Isa. 32:10,11.

- you will be troubled, Isa. 32:10, BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal IMPERFECT.
This term denotes "agitation," "shaking," "being perturbed." Note the "time" elements in Isa. 32:10.

- within a year and a few days

- time of the vintage is ended

- the fruit gathering will not come

- tremble, Isa. 32:11, BDB 353, KB 350, Qal IMPERATIVE,
cf. Isa. 10:29; 19:16; 41:5. This is parallel to "troubled" in Isa. 32:10 (surprisingly
all the IMPERATIVES of Isa. 32:11 are MASCULINE,
but addressed to women).

- be troubled, Isa. 32:11, BDB 919, KB 1182, Qal IMPERATIVE,
same VERB as Isa. 32:10

- strip, Isa. 32:11, BDB 832 II, KB 980, Qal IMPERATIVE. This
could be a sign of

- mourning (cf. Ezek. 26:16)

- humiliation (cf. Hosea 2:5)

- undress, Isa. 32:11, BDB 792, KB 889, Qal IMPERATIVE

- put sackcloth on your waist, Isa. 32:11, BDB 291, KB 291, Qal
IMPERATIVE, also a sign of mourning. See

SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES.

- beat your breasts, Isa. 32:12, BDB 704, KB 763, Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE,
another sign of mourning, Luke 18:13; 23:48.

All of these relate to the period of the siege of Jerusalem by Sennacherib in
701 B.C. Sieges were horrible experiences of deprivation and disease.

verses.zh: 无虑的女子啊，再过一年多，必受骚扰；因为无葡萄可摘，无果子（或译：禾稼）可收。
verses.en: In a year’s time[NOTE:1] you carefree ones will shake with fear,for the grape harvest[NOTE:2] will fail,and the fruit harvest will not arrive.
notes: Heb “days upon a year.”
Or perhaps, “olive.” See 24:13.
verses.commentary:
32:10 "Within a year and a few days" This is a very specific time reference (possibly connected
to the harvest season) and seems to relate to the invasion of Sennacherib in
701 B.C.

verses.zh: 安逸的妇女啊，要战兢；无虑的女子啊，要受骚扰。脱去衣服，赤着身体，腰束麻布。
verses.en: Tremble, you complacent ones!Shake with fear, you carefree ones!Strip off your clothes and expose yourselves—put sackcloth around your waists.[NOTE:1]
notes: The imperatival forms in v. 11 are problematic. The first (חִרְדוּ, khiredu, “tremble”) is masculine plural in form, though spoken to a feminine plural addressee (שַׁאֲנַנּוֹת, shaʾanannot, “complacent ones”). The four imperatival forms that follow (רְגָזָה, regazah, “shake with fear”; פְּשֹׁטָה, peshotah, “strip off your clothes”; עֹרָה, ʿorah, “expose yourselves”; and חֲגוֹרָה, khagorah, “put on”) all appear to be lengthened (so-called “emphatic”) masculine singular forms, even though they too appear to be spoken to a feminine plural addressee. GKC 131-32 §48.i suggests emending חִרְדוּ (khiredu) to חֲרָדָה (kharadah) and understanding all five imperatives as feminine plural “Aramaized” forms.

verses.zh: 她们必为美好的田地和多结果的葡萄树，捶胸哀哭。
verses.en: Mourn over the field,[NOTE:1] over the delightful fieldsand the fruitful vine.
notes: The Hebrew text has “over mourning breasts.” The reference to “breasts” would make sense in light of v. 11, which refers to the practice of women baring their breasts as a sign of sorrow (see J. N. Oswalt, Isaiah [NICOT], 1:585). However, one expects the preposition עַל (ʿal) to introduce the source or reason for mourning (see vv. 12b-13a) and the participle סֹפְדִים (sofedim, “mourning”) seems odd modifying “breasts.” The translation above assumes a twofold emendation: (1) שָׁדַיִם (shadayim, “breasts”) is emended to [ם]שָׂדַי (saday[m], “field,” a term that also appears in Isa 56:9). The final mem (ם) would be enclitic in this case, not a plural indicator. (The Hebrew noun שָׂדֶה (sadeh, “field”) forms its plural with an וֹת- [-ot] ending). (2) The plural participle סֹפְדִים is emended to סְפֹדָה (sefodah), a lengthened imperatival form, meaning “mourn.” For an overview of various suggestions that have been made for this difficult line, see Oswalt, 586, n. 12).
verses.commentary:
32:12 "Beat your breasts" There are three ways to deal with this phrase.

- relate it to the stripped and bare-breasted women of Isa. 32:11

- change the Hebrew "breast" (rare poetic term, BDB 994, שׁד)
to "fields" (BDB 961, שדי, cf. Isa. 56:9),
as JPSOA lists in a footnote. If option #2 is followed, then "fields," "the pleasant fields,"
and "the fruitful vine" become parallel for the loss of agricultural abundance.

- see it as an idiom for mourning whether male or female (Peshitta, cf. Luke 18:13; 23:48)

verses.zh: 荆棘蒺藜必长在我百姓的地上，又长在欢乐的城中和一切快乐的房屋上。
verses.en: Mourn[NOTE:1] over the land of my people,which is overgrown with thorns and briers,and over all the once-happy houses[NOTE:2] in the city filled with revelry.[NOTE:3]
notes: “Mourn” is supplied in the translation for stylistic reasons. In the Hebrew text vv. 12-13 are one long sentence.
Heb “indeed, over all the houses of joy.” It is not certain if this refers to individual homes or to places where parties and celebrations were held.
This same phrase is used in 22:2.
verses.commentary:
32:13 "the joyful houses" This same term "joyful" (BDB 965) is used in Isa. 32:14 for "a delight
for wild donkeys." Isaiah uses

- doubling

- word plays

- repeated metaphors

to communicate his messages. The Hebrew text of Isaiah is far more dynamic and artistic
than can be captured in translation. He was a master poet. One wonders if YHWH communicated the
messages in poetry or Isaiah crafted them. Since all of YHWH's revelations are not in artistic poetry, it
seems this was Isaiah's skill. Many of the word choices in Isaiah have far more to do with sound plays
than lexical meaning. Rare words are used, as are unique meanings to common words. This is where the
purposeful ambiguity is confusing for modern interpreters!

▣ "the jubilant city" See note at Isa. 24:10 and
SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TWO "CITIES"
IN ISAIAH. God wanted to uniquely bless the people of the Abrahamic covenant to attract the attention of "the nations,"
but because of Israel and Judah's rebellion, instead of abundance and peace came thorns and briars
(cf. Isa. 5:6; 7:23-25; 9:18; 10:17; 27:4; Gen. 3:18).

verses.zh: 因为宫殿必被撇下，多民的城必被离弃；山冈望楼永为洞穴，作野驴所喜乐的，为羊群的草场。
verses.en: For the fortress is neglected;the once-crowded[NOTE:1] city is abandoned.Hill[NOTE:2] and watchtowerare permanently uninhabited.[NOTE:3] Wild donkeys love to go there,and flocks graze there.[NOTE:4]
notes: Or “noisy” (NAB, NIV, NCV).
Hebrew עֹפֶל (ʿofel), probably refers here to a specific area within the city of Jerusalem. See HALOT 861 s.v. II עֹפֶל.

The Hebrew text has בְעַד מְעָרוֹת (veʿad meʿarot). The force of בְעַד, which usually means “behind, through, round about,” or “for the benefit of,” is uncertain here. HALOT 616 s.v. *מְעָרָה takes מְעָרוֹת (meʿarot) as a homonym of “cave” and defines it here as “cleared field.” Despite these lexical problems, the general point of the statement seems clear—the city will be uninhabited.
Heb “the joy of wild donkeys, a pasture for flocks.”
verses.commentary:
32:14 This verse describes the destruction of Jerusalem (cf. Isa. 6:11; 64:10), which is unusual
for Isaiah who usually sees its deliverance (cf. Isa. 1:8-9; 28:16; 29:1-8; 37:36-37). Isaiah asserts
Jerusalem's sanctity because of YHWH's presence there (i.e., the temple), but later Jeremiah clearly
adds to this theological issue by focusing on the conditional nature of YHWH's promises to His covenant
people (i.e., Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 27-28). Isaiah trusts God's word, but His promises must be
matched by appropriate human faith, repentance, obedience, service, worship. Covenant is a two-way street!

Notice how the destruction is characterized.

- the palace has been abandoned (i.e., the Davidic seed forsaken)

- the populated city has been forsaken (i.e., the Abrahamic seed forsaken)

- NASB ‒ "hill"

NJB ‒ "Ophel" (BDB 779), a section of the southeastern ridge of ancient Jerusalem
(or a metaphor for the whole city, similar to "Zion"). It is mentioned in 2 Chr. 27:3; 33:14;
Neh. 3:26-27; 11:21

- #3 is parallel to "watch-tower"; both would denote the fortifications of Jerusalem being destroyed

- a delight for wild donkeys

- a pasture for flocks, both #5 and #6 denote a deserted, destroyed city, inhabited only by animals
(cf. Isa. 13:21; 34:13)

There are two parallel VERBS.

- has been abandoned, BDB 643, KB 695, Pual PERFECT,
the Pual occurs only here

- forsaken, BDB 736, KB 806, Qal PASSIVE (or Pual)
PERFECT, cf. Jer. 49:25

The term (BDB 792) means "cave," but in this context, "an animal's den." It is possible
that Isaiah chose this term because of its sound similarity to

(context of death and destruction)

used in Isa. 32:11

(NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 1034)

▣ "forever" This is the relative use of the Hebrew term 'olam. This term has a large
semantical usage and must be interpreted in a specific context.

For a good example of the relative nature of 'olam (forever), notice the seeming
counteraction between v. 14, Jerusalem destroyed "forever," and v. 15, Jerusalem restored. Often "forever"
is used

- for intensity

- as hyperbole

- denoting a period of time

- this age (i.e. this covenant)

- eternity

Be careful of western literalism! Hebrew poetry and Eastern literature are far more figurative
than western thinking.

verses.zh: 等到圣灵从上浇灌我们，旷野就变为肥田，肥田看如树林。
verses.en: This desolation will continue[NOTE:1] until new life is poured out on us from heaven.[NOTE:2] Then the wilderness will become an orchard[NOTE:3]and the orchard will be considered a forest.[NOTE:4]
notes: The words “The desolation will continue” refer to the previous context and have been added for smoothness.

Heb “until a spirit is emptied out on us from on high.” The words “this desolation will continue” are supplied in the translation for clarification and stylistic purposes. The verb עָרָה (ʿarah), used here in the Niphal, normally means “lay bare, expose.” The term רוּחַ (ruakh, “spirit”) is often understood here as a reference to the divine spirit (cf. 44:3 and NASB, NIV, CEV, NLT), but it appears here without an article (cf. NRSV “a spirit”), pronominal suffix, or a genitive (such as “of the Lord”). The translation assumes that it carries an impersonal nuance “vivacity, vigor” in this context.

The term כַּרְמֶל (karmel) may refer to fertile land, an orchard, a garden of vines, a plantation of trees, or fresh grain. The dictionaries may subdivide these meaning under homonyms (see BDB 502, NIDOTTE 718, HALOT 499, The Concise DCH, 183). The picture of transformation is clearer when it is understood that a מִדְבָּר (midbar, “wilderness”) is an area that does not receive enough rainfall to support trees.

The same statement appears in 29:17b, where, in conjunction with the preceding line, it appears to picture a reversal. Here it seems to depict supernatural growth. The desert will blossom into an orchard, and the trees of the orchard will multiply and grow tall, becoming a forest.
verses.commentary:
32:15-20 This strophe describes a new day, a righteous day for Jerusalem.

- The Spirit is poured out from God. The exact relationship between YHWH and "the Spirit" in the OT
is difficult to relate to the full personal revelation of the NT. The Spirit is often associated
with creation (cf. Gen. 1:2; Job 26:13; Ps. 104:29-30). Now the Spirit is active in the new creation!

- The wilderness becomes a fertile field. . .a forest, Isa. 32:15. This is the reversal of Isa. 32:12-13.
See the same imagery of fertility in Isa. 29:17.

- Justice. . .righteousness abide, Isa. 32:16

- Peace, quietness, and confidence forever, Isa. 32:17. This means no invasions (cf. Isa. 32:18).

- Isa. 32:19 may refer to the destruction of Assyria.

- Isa. 32:20 is another blessing, but it is somewhat ambiguous.

SPECIAL TOPIC: PERSONHOOD OF THE SPIRIT

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE TRINITY

32:15

NASB, NKJV, NIV, Peshitta
"Until the Spirit is poured out upon us

from on high"

NKJV, JPSOA
"until a spirit from on high is poured

out on us"

TEV
"God will send us his spirit"

NJB
"until the spirit is poured out on us

from above"

Net Bible
"until new life is poured out on us

from heaven"

REB, LXX
"until a spirit from on high is lavished

upon me"

The Hebrew text has no ARTICLE, PRONOUN, or descriptive
phrase (i.e., "of the Lord," as in Isa. 11:2 or "My," Isa. 44:3; 59:21; Joel 2:28)
linked to the NOUN "spirit" (BDB 924). The question is to whom does it refer.

- the cultural spirit of the new age

- the Holy Spirit

- a spirit of faithful followers in repentance and trust from God

Grammar suggests #1 or #3, but context suggests #2.

This is a radical break in the context. Similar passages which speak of God's Spirit are
Isa. 44:3; Ezek. 39:29; Joel 2:28-29; Zech. 12:10; Acts 2:1-21. The same VERB
is used in a sacrificial sense of the Messiah in Isa. 53:12. There is a series of seven blessings that
will result because of the Spirit's presence: (1) fertility, (2) justice, (3) righteousness, (4) peace,
(5) quietness, (6) confidence, and (7) secure dwelling.

▣ "from on high" This is an idiom for "heaven," the place of YHWH's abode (cf. Job 16:19; 31:2;
Isa. 33:5).

verses.zh: 那时，公平要居在旷野；公义要居在肥田。
verses.en: Justice will settle down in the wildernessand fairness will live in the orchard.[NOTE:1]
notes: This new era of divine blessing will also include a moral/ethical transformation, as justice and fairness fill the land and replace the social injustice so prevalent in Isaiah’s time.
verses.commentary:
32:16 "justice. . .righteousness" These are a common pair in the OT (cf. 2 Sam. 8:15; 1 Kgs. 10:9;
1 Chr. 18:14; 2 Chr. 9:8; Ps. 99:4; Isa. 9:7; 32:16; 33:5; 59:14; Jer. 4:2; 9:24; 22:3,15; 23:5; 33:15;
Ezek. 18:5,19, 21,27; 33:14,16,19; 45:9; Amos 5:7,24). They denote the kind of society (cf. Isa. 32:17-18)
where all people are honored and treated fairly as covenant partners. They then characterize the unique
presence of God among His people.

verses.zh: 公义的果效必是平安；公义的效验必是平稳，直到永远。
verses.en: Fairness will produce peace[NOTE:1] and result in lasting security.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and the product of fairness will be peace.”
Heb “and the work of fairness [will be] calmness and security forever.”
verses.commentary:
32:17 "peace" See SPECIAL TOPIC: PEACE
(shalom, OT)

▣ "quietness and confidence" These two terms (BDB 1052 and BDB 105) also occur in Isa. 30:15,
which characterizes the new age of justice, righteousness, and peace (cf. Isa. 32:1,16).

verses.zh: 我的百姓必住在平安的居所，安稳的住处，平静的安歇所。
verses.en: My people will live in peaceful settlements,in secure homes,and in safe, quiet places.[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “in safe resting places”; NAB, NRSV “quiet resting places.”

verses.zh: （但要降冰雹打倒树林；城必全然拆平。）
verses.en: Even if the forest is destroyed[NOTE:1] and the city is annihilated,[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “and [?] when the forest descends.” The form וּבָרַד (uvarad) is often understood as an otherwise unattested denominative verb meaning “to hail” (HALOT 154 s.v. I ברד). In this case one might translate, “and it hails when the forest is destroyed” (cf. KJV, ASV, NASB, NIV). Perhaps the text alludes to a powerful wind and hail storm that knocks down limbs and trees. Some prefer to emend the form to וְיָרַד (veyarad), “and it descends,” which provides better, though not perfect, symmetry with the parallel line (cf. NAB). Perhaps וּבָרַד should be dismissed as dittographic. In this case the statement (“when the forest descends”) lacks a finite verb and seems incomplete, but perhaps it is subordinate to v. 20.
Heb “and in humiliation the city is laid low.”
verses.commentary:
32:19 This is a very difficult verse which seems out of place. It may refer to Assyria.

- The phrase "the forest" is used of Assyria in Isa. 10:18-19,33,34.

- The phrase "the city" is used of Assyria in Isa. 24:10; 25:2,3; 26:5.

The ancient versions see the MT's ברד,
BDB 135, "hail," cf. NOUN in Isa. 28:2,17; 30:30, which is related to an Arabic root
for "cool."

It is possible to see the MT as reflecting another root,
ירד, which means "to descend" or "come down"
(BDB 432, twice), denoting the complete destruction of faithless Jerusalem, NRSV, NJB, and JPSOA.

The UBS Text Project, p. 73, gives "hail" a "B" rating (some doubt).

verses.zh: 你们在各水边撒种、牧放牛驴的有福了！
verses.en: you will be blessed,you who plant seed by all the banks of the streams,[NOTE:1] you who let your ox and donkey graze.[NOTE:2]
notes: Heb “by all the waters.”

Heb “who set free the foot of the ox and donkey”; NIV “letting your cattle and donkeys range free.”sn This verse seems to anticipate a time when fertile land is available to cultivate and crops are so abundant that the farm animals can be allowed to graze freely.
verses.commentary:
32:20 This verse is also very difficult to fit into the context. However, the consensus seems to be
that in the days of God's blessings, the crops will be so abundant that the cattle could roam freely and
eat without really affecting the outcome of the crop.

D. Brent Sandy, Plowshares and Pruning Hooks: Rethinking the Language of Biblical Prophecy
and Apocalyptic, p. 23, gives a good list of the verses in Isaiah that speak of a new day of covenant prosperity.

- Isa. 2:4 ‒ swords turned into plowshares

- Isa. 29:18 ‒ blind see, deaf hear

- Isa. 30:25; 43:30 ‒ rivers flow in the desert

- Isa. 30:26 ‒ sun and moon shine brightly to aid agriculture

- Jer. 31:4,13; 33:11 ‒ sounds of community joy

- Isa. 32:20 ‒ livestock graze freely and the harvest is not negatively affected

- Isa. 34:16 ‒ every person will have a life partner (in context, this may refer to animals, Isa. 34:13-15)

- Isa. 35:1; 41:19 ‒ plant life returns to the desert

- Isa. 35:1; 41:18 ‒ pools of water collect in dry places

- Isa. 35:8 ‒ special highway of holiness provided by YHWH for His people

- Isa. 40:4 ‒ natural impediments (i.e. mountains and hills) removed (i.e. leveled) for easy access to YHWH

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which
means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible. Each of us must walk in the
light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not
relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare
your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing is not inspired, but it is
the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every
paragraph has one and only one subject.

CONTEXTUAL INSIGHTS

- Isaiah 31-32 are the fifth of the six woes (Isa. 28:1; 29:1,15; 30:1; 31:1; 33:1) which deal with
Hezekiah's attempt to form a political military alliance with the Nubian Pharaoh of the
Twenty-Fifth Dynasty of Egypt against Assyria.

- Judah trusted in Egypt, but not YHWH, for protection. Isaiah saw this as a violation of
trust/faith in His covenant promises and presence.

- This chapter focuses on the future government of a Righteous King in Jerusalem
(cf. Isa. 32:1; 9:6-7; 11:1-5; Micah 5:2-5a). This was what Hezekiah should have been. He
came close in his faith, seen in Isa. 37:14-20,30.

NASB (UPDATED) TEXT: ISAIAH 32:1-8

1Behold, a king will reign righteously

And princes will rule justly.

2Each will be like a refuge from the wind

And a shelter from the storm,

Like streams of water in a dry country,

Like the shade of a huge rock in a parched land.

3Then the eyes of those who see will not be blinded,

And the ears of those who hear will listen.

4The mind of the hasty will discern the truth,

And the tongue of the stammerers will hasten to speak clearly.

5No longer will the fool be called noble,

Or the rogue be spoken of as generous.

6For a fool speaks nonsense,

And his heart inclines toward wickedness:

To practice ungodliness and to speak error against the Lord,

To keep the hungry person unsatisfied

And to withhold drink from the thirsty.

7As for a rogue, his weapons are evil;

He devises wicked schemes

To destroy the afflicted with slander,

Even though the needy one speaks what is right.

8But the noble man devises noble plans;

And by noble plans he stands.
